Seminar Title:

Fabrication of Porous Si/C Hybrids with Nano Silicon and Engineered Carbon Frameworks for Li-Ion Battery Anodes

Abstract:

Silicon (Si) is one of the most promising anode materials for next-generation lithium-ion&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp batteries due to its exceptionally high theoretical capacity (~4200 mAh g-1). However, its practical application is hindered by severe volume expansion (upto 400%) during repeated lithiation and delithiation, leading to particle pulverization, unstable solid electrolyte interphase formation, and rapid capacity fading. This thesis addresses these challenges through the systematic design of porous silicon/carbon (Si/C) composite anodes by simultaneously engineering the carbon framework and pore architecture.

Initially, nanocrystalline Si was synthesized from micro-Si by high-energy mechanical milling using tungsten carbide milling media. Optimization of the milling parameters enabled the production of contamination-free Si nanoparticles with an average particle size of 45 nm and a crystallite size of 13 nm within 4 hours. The synthesized nano-Si served as the active material for the fabrication of porous Si/C composites. In the first approach, polymethylsilsesquioxane (PMS) was employed to generate a SiO2-rich SiOC sacrificial template, while in the second approach, freeze-dried colloidal SiO2 nanoparticles were used as hard templates to produce hierarchical porous architectures. In both approaches, coal tar pitch and phenolic resin were used as soft and hard carbon precursors, respectively, to systematically investigate the effect of carbon microstructure on electrochemical performance. Using PMS as a pore former, the porous Si/C composites prepared with coal tar pitch and phenolic resin as a carbon source delivered a reversible capacity of 863 mAh g-1 after 200 cycles and 874 mAh g-1 after 300 cycles, respectively, at 0.1 A g-1. Using freeze-dried colloidal SiO2 nanoparticles as a pore former, the coal tar pitch- and phenolic resin-derived porous Si/C composites delivered reversible capacities of 753 and 716 mAh g-1 after 400 cycles, respectively, at 0.1 A g-1. Finally, a template-free dual-polymer strategy employing polyvinylpyrrolidone as a pore phase and polyacrylonitrile as a carbon source was developed to prepare nitrogen-doped porous Si/C composites. The optimized Si/C composite exhibited an initial reversible capacity of 1029 mAh g-1 and retaining 805 mAh g-1 after 250 cycles at a higher current density of 1 A g-1.

The study establishes that carbon structure and pore-generation strategy play decisive roles in governing the microstructure and electrochemical performance of the Si/C anode. Carbon phase enhances the electrical conductivity, while engineered porosity accommodates volume changes, improves electrolyte infiltration, and facilitates Li-ion transport. This work presents a simple, scalable strategy for developing high-performance Si/C anodes for lithium-ion batteries.
